text: Precocious puberty (PP) is an important issue that affects approximately 1 in 5,000–10,000 children ( 1 , 2 ). In addition to physical problems, PP has been reported to be related to higher rates of psychological problems in patients when compared to healthy children ( 3 , 4 ). A previous longitudinal study of 2,607 girls with early menarche showed that early puberty might increase the risk of behavioral problems in young adolescent girls. Early maturing girls are at risk of persistently higher delinquency and stronger negative peer influences ( 5 ). These cognitive, behavioral, and emotional functioning changes are thought to be associated with specific brain development ( 6 – 8 ). However, few studies have specified the brain regions where particular maturational effects occur during this sensitive period within this special group. Identifying brain regions that contribute to psychological functioning in PP girls may be critical for interventions to prevent later negative outcomes.
